corrections.issue: Wrong speaker: the Barclay CTA index volatility figures (20-25% in the 1980s and early 1990s, below 5% now) are stated by the host Neils, interjecting after Katie. Katie only supplied the explanation that institutions entered and assets grew.
corrections.fix: Host Neils: the Barclay CTA index ran at 20-25% annualised volatility in the 1980s and early 1990s and is below 5% in recent years; Katie (preceding remark): institutional adoption and larger assets pushed managers toward lower-risk, size-management programmes.

corrections.issue: Speaker likely wrong: the host only introduces Jim at the end of C04 ('I certainly need to hear from Jim') and Jim starts with 'Yeah, look to take a step back'. The C03 speaker (agrees with Yov, cites the 6% US hedge fund allocation) is a different panelist, probably Andrew, and the transcript does not name him.
corrections.fix: Unnamed panelist (not Jim; possibly Andrew): managed futures is almost the only scalable, liquid strategy with zero correlation to stocks and bonds that pays off when needed, so a strategic allocation would be about 25%; pod shops come close but not as scalable.

corrections.issue: Same speaker problem as C03-3: attributed to Jim but the host brings Jim in only after this speaker finishes. Also the 30% figure is the managed futures share of the hedge fund sleeve ('from a 6 or 7% allocation to a 30% allocation which is where it should be'), which the claim states but attributes to Jim.
corrections.fix: Unnamed panelist (not Jim): US institutions hold about 6% in hedge funds with managed futures under 10% of that, roughly 50bp of the portfolio; benchmarked to hedge fund indices it is career-risky to raise managed futures from 6-7% to about 30% of the hedge fund sleeve, which is where it should be.

corrections.issue: Overstates what was said about diversification: the speaker says stocks and 60/40 each have a Sharpe of about 0.35, i.e. adding bonds gives zero diversification benefit, and calls the stock/bond approach zero diversification, rather than merely overstated.
corrections.fix: Jim: no allocator he asks can name the 125-year Sharpe of the S&P or of a 60/40 portfolio (both about 0.35), so bonds added no Sharpe benefit over stocks; yet 95% of investors diversify by holding more correlated assets, whereas true diversification comes from non-asset strategies such as trend following and long volatility.

completeness_estimate: 0.60 - the first reader caught the main TPA, process-stability, drawdown-structure and Sharpe/vol-compression arguments; it missed the AI-use remark, several allocator-behaviour mechanisms (narrative, iron spine, ETF drawdown visibility, no-single-event drawdowns, long vs deep), the Katie, Yov and Andrew 2026 predictions, and misattributed two C03 claims and the Barclay-vol statement.
